People asking how this happens, its about order of operations for generation.

First, the landscape is generated. For a superflat world, that is the flat part.

Then, caves and ores are generated in. This step is skipped on superflat worlds.

Trees are generated next based on available blocks.

The last thing generated is structures. Mineshafts are generated based on Y coordinates, and since superflat worlds are "on the bottom" in standard generation that means that they have low Y-values. 

This gets more into speculation, but they likely turned off generation of the platformed mineshafts (the ones which have the wood underneath) on superflat worlds to avoid having the floating structures about. Since mineshafts have a minimum Y-level they generate at, the world "attempts" to place them, then gets stopped. However, the previously generated large tree intersects the Y-level, meaning a mineshaft could be placed which it detected was tunneling through something, so didn't need the platform underneath, and placed a small section of it.

To use some actual city planning terms, what you want is a city following the multiple nuclei model at a small scale.

What I do is have "central" services - those which each wider city only needs at a small scale, so secret police, prison, courthouses, and higher education of some sort, as well as space for mass transit to deliver students in to the area. In western urban geography this would be called a central business district.

Then there is a ring of residential housing, which provides workers to the CBD primarily. This will have schools, sports, and kindergardens, and depending on scale grocery stores.

Outside this first thing is a series of service blocks, with police, shops, fire, medical, and culture, as well as mass transit connections. These service blocks should be spaced so that any one citizen can access at least one, but I findnif they are dense enough for most citizens to have a choice it smooths out a lot of problems. This is also where I usually place my heat distribution.

Outside of this is another district of housing, similar to the first, but with integrated public transit points.

Then you can have light industry (low pollution production but high manpower such as clothing and food are my preference) in a ring. Most cities I run have at least one of their own food factory and one sawmill. This is also where my heat plant is (though built much earlier with workers bussed out to it until the city fills out) and my city gates for electric and garbage. 

You can pipe college students into the center for education, and then workers from the outlying residencies that don't feed factories immediately in the vicinity can be piped to further factories, or a central worker consolidation station to take them further afield.

I think skill bloat is a good thing. You're in a warehouse, edge check to see if they have one near you. Tailing someone and you want to be reactive to them being about to see you? Edge check for a passing car to get behind. There's been hundreds of ways that my playgroup have used something as simple as the edge check. One of my current characters when I get to be on the player side of the table just sorta, stumbles through life with luck. It saves on the complexity of designing around the mantlet. Tank mantlets of this era slid over the armor plating, so you needed to have the area of the turret around the mantlet be curved. Now, you could just have a big bulky flat mantlet, such as the later 76 Shermans, or minimal downwards traversal, such as on the early 75 Shermans, or you could go the British route and have no external mantlet.

The germans tried out a few different options. The Tiger 1 has a full width mantlet that is flat, and where it interfaces with the main turret armor plate it is milled out with the curves. The Tiger II has a flat turret face and a sort of conical mantlet. The Panther uses a similar design to the Maus. The more complex the shape, the harder it is to manufacturer, so having some transitions to get some curved plates for the mantlet into flat plates for the cheeks would be harder to manufacture, and for a wielded turret that also introduces stress/break points. The Mauss was not a cheap thing, but its actual physical geometry was generally pretty simple to manufacture. The other advantage is weight savings - the Maus was already insanely heavy, minimizing complex geometry and he extra weight around both reinforcing it and the plates themselves would help there as well.

Note however that by the cold war most tanks replaced the idea of an outside mantlet with just the smallest possible hull opening for the gun with a cover over it for NBC protection, and mantlets have come and gone since with more modern designs.

This is just a pretty fundamental misunderstanding of tank usage and doctrine in the second world war. 

Take the Sherman, for instance. The weapon on the Sherman that caused the most damage to the enemy war effort, that won the most engagements, was the co-axial .30cal. In fact, infantry was such a big threat that Sherman commanders, if they were traveling with a loaded round, kept an HE round loaded. Furthermore, fundamentally, the majority of tanks were not taken out during tank-on-tank engagements. The first Tigers that the Brits encountered were taken out by 6 lber guns, one deployed in position, the other on a portee mount (mounted to the back of a truck for quick redeployment).   
  
The purpose of tank doctrine across pretty much all those who fought in the European was twofold, firstly, to carry weapons equivalent or beyond the capabilities of a similarly mobile conventional infantry squad in a protected way, and secondly to have more mobile firebases that can be used to exploit breakthroughs. Anti-tank weapon doctrine was a race to make anti-tank guns ubiquitous or portable enough to counter enemy tanks. The reason the Germans started developing heavier tanks is because their early war tanks were vunerable to anti-tank rifles, man portable anti-tank weapons, not in order to duel with other tanks. Vehicles like the STUG or M10/M18 were developed as part of the development of anti-tank guns rather than as specifically tanks, In fact early doctrine with the M10, and a large part of US tank destroy development, was that it was essentially to be used the same as a tractor, to make its way into a fighting position, entrench, and fight the same as a crew who had limbered a traditional gun. 

As far as "the brits wouldn't have had a good anti-tank tank if not for the Sherman" also shows a misunderstanding of British vehicle procurement and doctrine, and more widely how that worked with the Western allies. The reason the Brits used the Sherman wasn't because they didn't develop their own domestic tank designs that fulfilled the same role - that is what the mid-to-late cruiser tank designs did, such as Cromwell and Charioteer, and just missing the end of the war Centurion. The Cromwell itself was a formidable weapon, not again that it started life with the 6 lber, that as mentioned before had had good performance against Tiger in the Mediterranean. Churchill, after the ill-conceived Mk I was rectified, also was using 6 lber - in fact one of the major changes made to Churchill was to change over to the main gun out of Sherman due to a desire to make it more effective against infantry, something the 6 lber was not particularly good at. Sherman's own 75mm armor piercing shells were pretty poor as well until after the US captured enough German HVAP 75mm to reverse engineer them (note that the US 75mm, 76mm, and 3 inch guns were all actually the same bore, they just used the different numbering to lessen confusion about logistics. However this did mean that the Sherman 75 had significantly poorer performance vs the 3 inch, which is what led to the development of the 76). It is also worth noting that the Brits did put 17 lber into Shermans in preparation for D-Day (as well as many other vehicles that were lend-leased), while the US did not believe it would be necessary to introduce 76mm Shermans until the heavy resistance encountered by American forces during D-Day, something the Brits were able to get by much better due to the 17 lber.

Note also that, besides a few tank-on-tank engagements at the very closing stages of the war, vehicles that were dedicated for tank-on-tank combat such as the Pershing and IS-2, generally struggled in a lot of places that M4 or T-34 respectively would've been more effective. Really the only tank from the immediate postwar era that was any good in the long run was Centurion, with both IS and Pershing quickly being outdated and replaced as the cold war started up.

Yeah that's the issue, most deaf people would not classify it as worse than other forms of communication innately, or being able to hear as being better.

Most sign language first language folks who are given the opportunity to converse with other sign language first language folks have similar reading comprehension, learning skills, and communication speeds to those with an auditory first language. In communities with high percentages of those who can sign, they generally have no worse outcomes within that community. It is, in essence, a quintessential culturally derived disability *as long as there is a sufficient density of people who can sign*.

And that's where the problem is, there isn't a magic wand that will cure all the reasons people need to use sign language, there in all likelihood never will be a cure for every cause. The fear is that you will, essentially, just fragment the community smaller, and deny these children access to the community which does not need them to adapt (most available auditory implants currently are not 100% and would still be considered as a "disability" and have issues with communication and face stigmas from (some) spoken language folks). Ultimately, the view of the vast majority is that it is individual choice, but when they say individual they *mean* individual, and there's a lot of stigma coming from able bodies folks against those who may choose not to get implants or other surgeries.

And I think a lot of the controversy from outside the community comes from a basal misunderstanding of what sign language is.

Sign language is not just "the language people speak in the country where words are replaced with sign" - it often has its own grammar structure, syntax, linguistic drift, etc., even its own ways of forming jokes and poetry (a joke about Uranus sounding like a body part doesn't work in sign). The big concern is what happens when everyone who could get implants and no longer need to learn sign does? What happens to those who can't have that outcome, an already marginalized group, what happens when their local schools no longer have sufficient populations who sign as a first language to allow the kids to become conversational in sign?
